clue.text: Put money in to settle account for programme of entertainment .

indicators.note: the clue tells us to put the money letter in, so it goes inside the phrase for settling up

parts.note: to settle an account is to pay the bill
L is the abbreviation for pound (librum), a unit of money

explanation.surface: A theatregoer pays their tab before picking up the evening's programme, which runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put ... in' is the container signal: L goes inside PAY BILL. The trailing dots carry the sentence on into 5 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: A playbill is a poster or printed sheet listing a show and its cast.

clue.text: A grip for a shopping item

explanation.surface: Someone looks for something to hold on to while out shopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchase means a firm hold or leverage, and also a thing bought.

clue.text: Sailors in a spot getting decoration

indicators.note: in places the sailors inside the word for spot

parts.note: a dot is a small spot
RN men are men of the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Sailors in a tight corner earn a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spot' suggests trouble; it is a DOT, with RN (Royal Navy) MEN inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An adornment is an ornament or embellishment.

clue.text: It's a metal club that's been stolen

indicators.note: been stolen means the letters for that is are taken away from the club

parts.note: a brassie is an old golf club
that's is that is, abbreviated i.e.

explanation.surface: A golfer's metal club has been nicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' expands to 'that is', i.e., which is lifted out of BRASSIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, loosely a metal.

clue.text: Talk in City square an attraction? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: in says one part goes inside another in the clue's order of mention
this phrase flips the in instruction, so the attraction holds the City and square rather than sitting in them

parts.note: a lure is an attraction or bait
EC is the postcode for the City of London
a T-square is a drawing tool, so square gives T

explanation.surface: A speech about whether a London square is a draw for visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the attraction goes in EC T; 'Quite the reverse' puts EC T inside LURE instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A lecture is a formal talk to an audience.

clue.text: … and put paid to drink

explanation.surface: Following on from 1 Across, someone settles up and then finishes off a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening dots tie this clue to 1 Across, so the 'and' merely continues that sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To put paid to something is to stop or crush it, as one scotches a rumour; Scotch is also whisky from Scotland, a drink.

clue.text: A hundred attending instruction is a crowd

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
on means attending, as in on duty or on a course
a course is a programme of instruction

explanation.surface: A hundred people turn up to a training session, making a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A concourse is a throng of people gathered together.

clue.text: First class art in reconstruction of Crown jewels

indicators.note: reconstruction means rebuilding, so these letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: A1 means first class, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A first-rate restorer works on the royal regalia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crown jewels' suggests the royal collection; it means jewels for the crown of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled head ornament, a small crown.

clue.text: Two little boys walked unsteadily

parts.note: Hal is short for Harry or Henry
Ted is short for Edward

explanation.surface: Two toddlers totter about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little boys' means boys' names in short forms.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt, in the old sense, is to limp or move unsteadily.

clue.text: Brave man on board surmounting extremes of exposure

indicators.note: in a down entry, surmounting puts the chess piece on top of what follows

parts.note: a pawn is a chess man on the board

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A brave chess player risks overexposure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' is a noun: a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pawnee are a Native American people of the Great Plains; a warrior is traditionally called a brave.

clue.text: Girl's letter from Greece, "Send back our Times"

parts.note: rho is the seventeenth letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: sending something back here asks us to write the following abbreviation backwards

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, labels the dates of our own era

explanation.surface: A girl writes home from Greece asking for copies of The Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Girl's' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. 'Send back' turns AD into DA.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhoda is a female given name.

clue.text: Secure post that gives cover against personal injury

parts.note: to chain something up is to secure it
post and mail both mean letters delivered

explanation.surface: An insurance advert: a safe job that provides accident cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a job with insurance benefits; 'post' is letters, and the cover is literal armour.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain mail is armour of linked metal rings worn to protect the body from blows.

clue.text: Minimal effort attributable to Workers Act

parts.note: hands are labourers, as in farmhands or factory hands
a turn is an act or performance on stage

explanation.surface: Laziness blamed on a piece of employment legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers Act' reads like the name of a law; it is two separate pieces, and 'attributable to' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand's turn is the least bit of work, as in 'he never did a hand's turn'.

clue.text: Spout has no value

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing, so it stands for no
a rate is a value or price set on something

explanation.surface: A spout, such as a jug's, judged worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like a noun but is the verb: to speak pompously.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to hold forth at length, much as someone spouts.

clue.text: Set out to annoy with fruitless result

indicators.note: out here signals the letters of the first word are put out of order

parts.note: to rile someone is to annoy them

explanation.surface: Someone set out to irritate and got nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SET into STE, then RILE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile means producing nothing, barren, unproductive.

clue.text: Fool may be amusing or awful

indicators.note: awful suggests something badly made, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clown can be funny or dreadful.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant person, a dunce.

clue.text: Occasion to see red and green — a funny mixture

indicators.note: a funny mixture is an odd jumble, so the letters before it are scrambled

explanation.surface: A colour-blindness test, or a paint pot where red and green get mixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasion' is a verb meaning cause. The letters of GREEN and A are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrage someone is to cause them fury, making them see red.

clue.text: Let design run wild — it showed sparkle

indicators.note: letters allowed to run wild are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A designer's freewheeling creation proved brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: Glistened means shone or glittered.

clue.text: Painter not noted for seascapes perhaps

definitions.text: Painter not noted for seascapes perhaps

parts.words: Painter not noted for seascapes perhaps
parts.note: a Victorian artist famed for animals; split up, the surname suggests a visionary of dry ground rather than the sea

explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edwin Landseer was a British artist famous for his animal paintings and the lions in Trafalgar Square.

clue.text: No sign of stress, but requiring pick-me-up

explanation.surface: Someone appears calm but could do with a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as 'a tonic', something a person in need of a pick-me-up requires.
explanation.definitionFit: An atonic syllable carries no accent; split in two, the word names a restorative drink, the tonic someone feeling low needs.

clue.text: "When beggars die there are no _____ seen" (J Caesar)

definitions.text: "When beggars die there are no _____ seen" (J Caesar)

parts.words: "When beggars die there are no _____ seen" (J Caesar)
parts.note: a line from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, spoken by Calpurnia, about portents in the sky foretelling the death of princes

explanation.definitionFit: Calpurnia's line goes on to say the heavens blaze forth the death of princes; the missing word names those blazing celestial objects.

clue.text: Heather follows mother back across the Atlantic

indicators.note: follows places the plant word after the reversed parent word
back here means the word for mother is to be written in reverse

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
erica is the botanical name for heather

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather emigrates to join her mother over the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a name; it is the plant. 'back' turns MA into AM.
explanation.definitionFit: From a British viewpoint, the United States lies over the Atlantic Ocean.

clue.text: Dog by Rodin an aberration

indicators.note: an aberration is a departure from the normal, so the letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A sculpture of a dog by Rodin is a misstep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is not an animal but a firedog.
explanation.definitionFit: A firedog is one of a pair of metal stands that hold logs in a hearth.

clue.text: Keep quiet — don't allow a breeze

explanation.surface: Someone told to shush and shut the window.
explanation.walkthrough: Split, the answer is an order to keep quiet; whole, it means to leave a sailing ship without wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Be calm is an order to stay still; to becalm a ship is to leave it windless.

clue.text: Go into business without using force

indicators.note: without tells us to drop the force word from the business word

parts.note: an enterprise is a business venture
to prise is to force something open with a lever

explanation.surface: Advice to break into a market without strong-arm tactics.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a place is to go inside it.

clue.text: Row in which many watch, maybe

indicators.note: in which puts the many letter inside the row word

parts.note: a tier is a row of seats
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: A row of seats where a crowd watches a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watch' looks like a verb; it is a noun, an example of a timepiece, hence 'maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch is a kind of timepiece, measuring the passing of minutes.

clue.text: Went down middle of road with dangerous beginner

parts.note: middle-of-the-road politics are moderate

indicators.note: the beginner of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A driver weaved down the centre of the road, a reckless learner at the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle of road' is not a letter pick but a phrase meaning moderate; 'beginner' takes D from 'dangerous'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something moderated has eased or lessened, as a storm subsides.

clue.text: A bad sport

parts.note: reads as a sore loser, but is a plant that varies from type, which gardeners call a sport, and also a scoundrel

explanation.definitionFit: In horticulture a plant deviating from its variety is weeded out; the word also means a rascal.

clue.text: Two scholars in reform school, perhaps

indicators.note: in places the scholars inside the word for reform

parts.note: to alter something is to change or reform it

indicators.note: two asks for the scholar abbreviation twice

parts.note: an MA is a Master of Arts, a scholar's degree

explanation.surface: Two pupils are sent to a reform school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform school' reads as one phrase, but 'reform' is ALTER and 'school, perhaps' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: One's alma mater is the school or university one attended; the 'perhaps' allows for a college.

clue.text: Bottled spirit?

parts.note: reads as a spirit like gin in a bottle, but means a supernatural being kept in a lamp or bottle, as in the Arabian Nights

explanation.definitionFit: A jinni of Arabian legend is often shut inside a lamp or bottle until released.

clue.text: Doctor got up — on the wrong side of the bed?

definitions.text: on the wrong side of the bed?

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor
rose means got up out of bed

explanation.surface: A doctor got out of bed grumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone who got out of bed on the wrong side is sullen; the question mark marks the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloomy and sullen is how someone who got up on the wrong side of the bed feels.

clue.text: English directions to the German father

parts.note: E and N, east and north, are compass directions
der is the masculine German word for the

explanation.surface: An English person gives directions to a German man's father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'father' is a verb at the end, not a noun; 'the German' is DER.
explanation.definitionFit: To father something is to beget or produce it, the same as to bring it about.
